Correctness::Duplicate event handling.summary: Make payment fulfillment idempotent: repeated or concurrent calls for the same Checkout Session must not grant goods twice. Deduplicate deliveries and check payment_status before fulfilling.
Correctness::Duplicate event handling.explanation: Stripe can invoke fulfillment repeatedly and concurrently for one Checkout Session. Store processed event IDs durably, ignore already-recorded deliveries, and verify payment_status before performing fulfillment so retries cannot grant goods twice.

parameters.name: sessionId
parameters.description: Checkout Session ID passed to the fulfillment function.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: Stripe webhook event supplied to the event handler.

Correctness::Duplicate event handling.returns: A successful webhook handler should return HTTP 200 after processing or skipping the event.

Use the Checkout Session ID as the fulfillment identity and safely handle repeated calls.
Use checkout.session.completed as a payment event that can trigger fulfillment.
gotchas: A webhook can receive duplicate deliveries, so deduplicate using recorded event IDs.
Already-processed events should be skipped and acknowledged successfully to prevent further retries.
Event IDs alone may not identify logically duplicated notifications; compare the data object ID and event type when applicable.
Do not assume webhook events arrive in creation order.

Correctness::Idempotency keys.summary: Send a unique idempotency key when creating or updating a Stripe object. If a connection failure leads to a retry, reuse the same key and parameters so Stripe does not perform the operation twice.
Correctness::Idempotency keys.explanation: Generate a unique key for a create request and send it in the Idempotency-Key request option. If the request must be retried, reuse that key with the identical endpoint and parameters; Stripe returns the stored result rather than performing the operation again. This protects payment creation from duplicate execution after connection failures.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: A unique client-generated value sent with the request options as Idempotency-Key; use the same value for an identical retry. Maximum length is 255 characters.

parameters.name: Request endpoint and parameters
parameters.description: The original request endpoint and parameters; retries using the key must match them.

Correctness::Idempotency keys.returns: Stripe saves the first request’s status code and response body for the key; later identical requests return that same result, including 500 errors.

example.title: Create a PaymentIntent safely
example.explanation: Creates a PaymentIntent with a unique key that can be reused for an identical retry.

useCases.title: Safe payment creation retry
useCases.scenario: Retrying a PaymentIntent creation after a connection failure without risking a second payment operation.

useCases.title: Unknown request outcome
useCases.scenario: Repeating a POST request when the client cannot determine whether the original request completed.

useCases.title: Duplicate-operation prevention
useCases.scenario: Protecting object creation or updates from duplicate execution during network retries.

keyPoints: Idempotency keys let a client retry a request without unintentionally repeating the operation.
Attach a key when creating or updating Stripe objects, including payment creation requests.
The client chooses the key; Stripe uses it to identify retries belonging to the original request.
Generate keys with sufficient randomness, such as UUID v4, so separate operations do not accidentally share a key.
Keep each key within Stripe’s 255-character maximum.
Stripe API POST requests accept idempotency keys.
gotchas: Reuse a key only for the same endpoint and parameters; changing either can cause an idempotency error.
Do not depend on the key preventing duplication indefinitely: after Stripe removes an older key, reuse can start a new operation.
Use keys for mutating requests such as POST; they provide no benefit for GET or DELETE.

Correctness::Race conditions.summary: Stripe doesn’t guarantee webhook event order, so a dependent event can arrive before your local record exists. Make processing order-independent, deduplicate by event ID, and retrieve missing Stripe objects through the API.
Correctness::Race conditions.explanation: Stripe can deliver related events in an order different from their creation order, so webhook processing must not assume that an earlier event—or your local record—already exists. Acknowledge deliveries quickly, process them asynchronously, deduplicate by event ID, and retrieve missing Stripe objects through the API when needed.

example.title: Acknowledge and queue a webhook
example.explanation: Acknowledge the webhook promptly, then enqueue it for asynchronous, idempotent processing that can retrieve missing Stripe objects when necessary.

useCases.title: Bridge webhook and database races

useCases.title: Process unordered event streams
useCases.scenario: Related Stripe events are delivered in a different order than they were created.

useCases.title: Make webhook handling idempotent
useCases.scenario: Stripe retries an event or sends a duplicate delivery.

keyPoints: Treat webhook delivery as unordered: a dependent event can arrive before the event that created your application record.
Design handlers so each event can be processed safely even when prerequisite events have not arrived.
If a webhook references data missing locally, retrieve the current Stripe object through the API instead of failing permanently.
Do not infer a reliable sequence from equal or nearby creation timestamps.
gotchas: Do not make processing depend on event arrival order; a webhook may arrive before the local record or related event is available.
Timestamps are not a safe ordering or deduplication mechanism.

Correctness::Signature verification.sourceTitle: How to ensure security in Stripe webhooks?
Correctness::Signature verification.summary: Verify every Stripe webhook before acting on it. Use the raw request body, Stripe-Signature header, and the endpoint's signing secret with Stripe's official library.
Correctness::Signature verification.explanation: Stripe signs each webhook with the Stripe-Signature header. Pass the unmodified UTF-8 request body, that header, and the endpoint's whsec_ signing secret to the official library's constructEvent function; process the event only when verification succeeds.

parameters.description: The unmodified request body string sent by Stripe.

parameters.description: The Stripe-Signature request header.

parameters.name: endpointSecret
parameters.description: The endpoint-specific webhook signing secret, beginning with whsec_.

Correctness::Signature verification.returns: A verified Stripe Event when the signature is valid; otherwise the verification function throws an error.

Prefer Stripe's official SDK verification helpers instead of implementing cryptography yourself.
Verification requires the raw payload, signature header, and endpoint signing secret.
Reject the request and do not perform webhook side effects when verification fails.
gotchas: Do not parse, reserialize, or otherwise modify the request body before verification; body changes make verification fail.
Framework middleware such as JSON parsing must not run before the webhook route.

Correctness::Webhook fulfilment.summary: Use Stripe’s webhook event as the authoritative server-side signal to fulfill an order. Do not rely on the customer’s redirect or client-side state, because the customer can leave before fulfillment starts.
Correctness::Webhook fulfilment.explanation: Stripe recommends using a server-side webhook rather than client-side completion or redirects to drive fulfillment. Listen for the relevant payment event, verify its signature, acknowledge the request promptly, and make fulfillment idempotent so retries cannot duplicate delivery.
Correctness::Webhook fulfilment.returns: A successful 2xx HTTP response to acknowledge receipt of the webhook; fulfillment is performed asynchronously on the server.

For Checkout, handle checkout.session.completed and use the session data to perform fulfillment.
Expose a server endpoint that receives Stripe events and confirms successful receipt.
Keep fulfillment logic in a server-side function invoked by the webhook handler.

Lifecycle operations::Disputes and charg.summary: A dispute reverses a payment and debits your Stripe balance. Review it before the deadline, then accept it or challenge it with relevant evidence; the issuing bank decides the outcome.
Lifecycle operations::Disputes and charg.explanation: A dispute, also called a chargeback, reverses the payment and debits the payment amount plus any dispute fee from the Stripe balance. Review the dispute before its deadline, then either accept it or challenge it by submitting relevant evidence; the submitted response is final. If the dispute is won, the reversed funds are returned.
Lifecycle operations::Disputes and charg.returns: The page describes dispute handling and evidence submission; it does not define a single function return value.

keyPoints: A chargeback begins when the cardholder challenges a payment with the issuing bank.
Stripe immediately reverses the payment and removes the amount plus applicable network fees.
The response window is network-dependent and commonly lasts 7–21 days.
Accept the dispute when you do not intend to contest the debit.
Challenge a dispute by providing evidence tailored to its reason and response type.
gotchas: Treat the response deadline as mandatory; missing it causes an automatic loss.
Submitting evidence is irreversible, so verify the evidence and explanation before submission.
An inquiry and a chargeback are different stages; a later chargeback requires its own response.

Lifecycle operations::Failed payments an.summary: Configure Smart Retries or custom schedules to recover failed renewal payments, notify customers, and choose what happens when retries are exhausted. Stripe can cancel, mark the subscription unpaid, leave it past_due, or pause it, depending on the dunning settings.
Lifecycle operations::Failed payments an.explanation: When a renewal payment fails, a charge-automatically subscription becomes past_due. Stripe then retries according to Smart Retries or a custom schedule and can expose the next attempt through next_payment_attempt. If recovery still fails, the configured dunning end action moves the subscription to canceled, unpaid, past_due, or paused. Use the invoice.payment_failed webhook to monitor failures and retry updates, and communicate with the customer or collect a new payment method.
Lifecycle operations::Failed payments an.returns: A subscription with a payment-failure status and an invoice that may expose the next collection attempt; after retries, the subscription follows the configured dunning end action.

keyPoints: Stripe recommends eight retry attempts over two weeks as the default Smart Retry policy.
The invoice’s next_payment_attempt field identifies when Stripe plans the next collection attempt.
Handle invoice.payment_failed to observe renewal failures and changes to retry attempts.
gotchas: Use the invoice’s next_payment_attempt value when displaying or scheduling around the next retry.

Lifecycle operations::Invoices and recei.sourceTitle: Receipts and paid invoices - Stripe Documentation
Lifecycle operations::Invoices and recei.summary: Stripe creates receipts for successful payments and refunds. Enable invoice creation for one-time Checkout payments when customers need a paid invoice with more detail than a standard receipt.
Lifecycle operations::Invoices and recei.explanation: Stripe creates receipts for successful payments and refunds. For one-time Checkout payments, enable invoice creation to produce a paid invoice with more detail than a standard receipt; after successful payment, Stripe emails links to download both documents. Use the Charge object's receipt_url when the application needs to link directly to the receipt.

parameters.description: Checkout Session creation parameter that enables invoice creation for a one-time payment.

Use a paid invoice when customers need richer documentation than a standard payment receipt.
Subscription invoices are automatic; enable invoice creation explicitly for one-time Checkout payments.
Link customers directly to a receipt with the Charge object's receipt_url value.

Receipts are browser-viewable, allowing an application to present or link to them without generating its own document.

Lifecycle operations::Refunds.summary: Create full or partial refunds through Stripe's Refunds API using a Charge or PaymentIntent. Track the returned Refund and its status in your records.
Lifecycle operations::Refunds.explanation: Create a Refund using the payment's PaymentIntent or Charge identifier. Omitting the amount refunds the remaining charge in full; supplying a positive amount in the currency's smallest unit creates a partial refund. Multiple refunds are allowed until the original charge is fully refunded, after which further refunds fail. Store the returned Refund identifier and status so your records can follow the operation.

Identify the payment with either its PaymentIntent ID or Charge ID.
The API supports full refunds, partial refunds, and multiple refunds for one charge.
Each refund is limited to the amount that remains unrefunded.
gotchas: The sum of all refunds cannot exceed the original charge amount.
Refunds draw from the available Stripe balance rather than the pending balance.
A fully refunded charge cannot receive another refund.

Lifecycle operations::Subscriptions.sourceTitle: Create a subscription | Stripe API Reference
Lifecycle operations::Subscriptions.summary: Subscriptions charge customers for products at recurring prices. Trials delay the first charge, while upgrades, downgrades, and quantity changes can create prorations that are invoiced immediately or later.
Lifecycle operations::Subscriptions.explanation: A subscription charges a customer repeatedly for a product at its configured price. Changes such as switching prices or quantities can create prorations; choose whether Stripe invoices them immediately, defers them, or omits them, while trial settings delay the first charge.

Operating & compliance::Key management.summary: Separate publishable keys for client-side code from secret keys for servers. Store secrets securely and rotate them periodically or immediately after exposure, saving each replacement because it cannot be retrieved later.
Operating & compliance::Key management.explanation: Use publishable keys in client-side code and keep secret keys on your server. Store secrets in a vault or environment variable, rotate them periodically, and immediately replace any exposed or compromised secret key. In the Dashboard, rotation revokes the old key and creates a replacement; copy and save the replacement because it cannot be retrieved later.

keyPoints: Publishable keys are intended for browser or app clients, while secret keys belong only in the server environment.
Prefer a platform secrets vault to provide secret keys to the integration at runtime.
When no vault is available, pass the secret through an environment variable.
Establish and practice periodic rotation so the team knows where each key is used and can replace it quickly.
Dashboard rotation invalidates the old key and creates a replacement that can be used immediately.
Choose immediate rotation or schedule expiration for the old key when the migration plan requires a transition period.
gotchas: Save a newly generated or rotated key immediately; Stripe does not let you retrieve its value later.
Rotate an exposed or compromised restricted or secret key immediately, even when you are unsure whether it was accessed.
Do not commit secret keys to source code or repositories; supply them through a secrets vault or environment variable.
Do not embed secret keys in distributed applications; use publishable keys for client-side integrations.

Operating & compliance::PCI scope.summary: Keep raw card details out of your servers by collecting and transmitting them directly to Stripe with a low-risk integration. This reduces PCI DSS obligations, but PCI compliance remains shared between Stripe and your business.
Operating & compliance::PCI scope.explanation: PCI DSS applies to organizations that store, process, or transmit card data. A low-risk Stripe integration collects and sends payment information directly to Stripe, so raw card details do not pass through your servers and your PCI obligations are reduced. Stripe may return non-sensitive details such as the card brand and last four digits, which the documentation says can be stored.

keyPoints: Your PCI responsibilities depend on whether your systems process, transmit, or store cardholder data.
Prefer Stripe integrations that keep raw payment details out of your backend.
Direct-to-Stripe collection reduces the amount of PCI work your environment must cover.
Stripe-returned non-sensitive card details can be retained for display or reconciliation.
gotchas: Handling untokenized card data yourself can require substantially more PCI DSS controls.
Using Stripe does not remove your responsibility to maintain PCI compliance and attest to it.

Operating & compliance::Reconciliation.summary: Reconcile each Stripe payout with the complete batch of balance transactions it settles. Use the payout ID to retrieve those transactions and compare them with your internal ledger.
Operating & compliance::Reconciliation.explanation: Payout reconciliation matches a Stripe payout with the payments, refunds, disputes, fees, and other balance transactions included in that payout. Retrieve the payout’s associated Balance Transactions, then compare their amounts and statuses with your internal ledger; the report also exposes balances and transactions that remain unsettled at the report end date.

Use the balance summary to compare Stripe’s opening and closing balances with the corresponding period in your ledger.

Operating & compliance::Taxes and region.summary: Stripe Tax helps calculate and collect indirect taxes according to regional obligations. Register in each jurisdiction, add registrations to Stripe, and enable automatic tax in your payment integration.
Operating & compliance::Taxes and region.explanation: Stripe Tax determines applicable tax using your business location, tax registrations, product tax codes, customer location, and customer status. First register with the relevant tax authorities and add those registrations to Stripe; then enable automatic tax in the payment integration so Stripe calculates tax only in jurisdictions where you are registered.

Automatic tax does not calculate tax for regions without an active Stripe registration.

Payment flow::Authentication and 3-D Sec.summary: 3D Secure adds an issuer-controlled authentication step when Stripe determines a card transaction needs extra verification. Integrations must support the resulting customer challenge and then handle the updated payment status.
Payment flow::Authentication and 3-D Sec.explanation: Stripe evaluates a card payment for 3DS based on regulations, Radar rules, explicit requests, issuer soft declines, and other factors. If authentication is needed, Stripe starts the issuer flow and the customer completes the challenge; your integration then handles the resulting PaymentIntent status.

keyPoints: Stripe decides whether 3DS is supported and required using regulations, Radar, explicit API requests, issuer soft declines, and other signals.
When authentication is required, Stripe contacts the issuer’s ACS to begin the 3DS flow.
You can request 3DS explicitly on a PaymentIntent, SetupIntent, or Checkout Session with the card payment method option.

Stripe.js can present the issuer authentication interface when these client-side methods are used.
gotchas: A customer challenge is not guaranteed: Stripe prompts for authentication only when 3DS is available for that card.
Do not assume every unavailable or failed 3DS attempt automatically means the payment is declined; Stripe may continue the payment normally.
